quotes.quote: For similarly there are commanded to be placed upon the altar "these fats of the ram which are around the kidneys, and those which cover the inward parts"; so that you too, who hear these things, may know that everything within you that is grosser and covers your "inward parts" you ought to offer to the fire of the altar, so that all your "inward parts" may be purged, and you too may say, as David also said: "bless the Lord, O my soul, and all my inward parts his holy name". For unless that grossness which covers your "inward parts" is removed, they cannot grasp a subtle and spiritual sense, nor can they grasp the understanding of wisdom, and therefore they cannot praise the Lord.

"Hear my prayer, O God, and my supplication; give ear to my tears". It is fitting once again to offer prayer to God even with tears, and to be moved from the innermost recesses into supplication of the Lord, so that the mind, believing in the judgment to come, may review the recollection of its misdeeds not without tears and lamentation. Who, dissolved into tears, says to the Lord: "I pour out my prayer in your sight"? "Give ear, therefore, to my tears, and be not silent", he says, "from me"—that is, while I pray be not silent. But what then? While I am still speaking, say: Behold, I am here.

"For I am a sojourner with you, and a pilgrim, as all my fathers". Because I am a pilgrim, I am necessarily also a sojourner, for I am not as you are. For you alone are eternal, and we, as far as is found, have a beginning. But I, if I be made worthy to be with you, am nevertheless a sojourner and a pilgrim with you; because all my fathers too were sojourners and pilgrims with you; and Abraham is a pilgrim with you, because he did not always exist, but then began to exist when you willed, and so Isaac and Jacob and all the righteous.

This is not the time to prove that the Creator did not become the servant of the Word and make the world and to show that the Word became the servant of the creator and prepared the world. For according to the prophet David, "God spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created." For the uncreated God "commanded" the firstborn of all creation, and "they were created." This includes not only the cosmos and the things in it, but also all that remains, "whether thrones, or dominations, or principalities or powers; for all things have been created through him and for him, and he is before all things."
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 2:104

quotes.quote: "Turn aside from evil and do good, and dwell forever and ever". Hearing these things, he says, do what is good, thou shalt dwell forever — that is, if thou shalt act as thou hast been taught, thy dwelling shall be eternal. For if thou look not to the things that are seen, but to the things that are not seen — since the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal — thou shalt dwell forever.

Celsus has not explained how error accompanies the "becoming," or product of generation; nor has he expressed himself with sufficient clearness to enable us to compare his ideas with ours, and to pass judgment on them. But the prophets, who have given some wise suggestions on the subject of things produced by generation, tell us that a sacrifice for sin was offered even for new-born infants, as not being free from sin. They say, "I was shapen in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me;" also, "They are estranged from the womb;" which is followed by the singular expression, "They go astray as soon as they are born, speaking lies."

But if it pleases you to hear what the other saints also thought concerning that nativity, hear David saying: "In iniquities," he says, "was I conceived, and in sins did my mother bear me," showing that whatever soul is born in the flesh is polluted with the filth "of iniquity and sin"; and that on this account was said what we have already mentioned above, that: "No one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day." To these things this too may be added, that it be inquired what is the cause that, whereas the baptism of the Church is given for the remission of sins, according to the observance of the Church baptism is given even to little children; when indeed, if there were nothing in little children that ought to pertain to remission and indulgence, the grace of baptism would seem superfluous.

"From all my iniquities deliver me". He necessarily added "from all", so that of course no iniquity may hold and constrain us. But let us consider how God delivers from iniquities. If, repenting for our evil deeds, we turn to God, God, receiving our conversion from us, grants absolution of iniquities according to the measure of the conversion. For to whom more is remitted, loves more; and therefore it is said of that woman that "much was remitted to her, because she loved much". According to the measure of the repentance, then, the quantity of remission is regulated; let us not deceive ourselves, thinking that these things are dispensed by no rules, by no judgments. For I think that he who has fulfilled all righteousnesses washes away all iniquities; but he who has worked few, or some part of righteousness, dissolves some part of his iniquities; and he who has borne perfect and entire…

"You have made me a reproach to the foolish". As long as we have sins, it is necessary that we be reproached by the foolish one and our accuser, the devil; and if our sins are found not to be blotted out, but written in us by the pen of the devil, through these very things which we have done the enemy will reproach us. For just as all good things are said to be written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, so all evil things are written down with the ink and pen of the devil. On account of which our Lord and Savior blotted out the handwriting of our sins, which was written against us with the devil's endorsement, just as he had also foretold before through the prophet who said: "Behold, I blot out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist, and I will no longer remember them". Therefore, that we may not be reproached by the foolish one, let us turn ourselves…

And he prays "constantly" (deeds of virtue or fulfilling the commandments are included as part of prayer) who unites prayer with the deeds required and right deeds with prayer. For the only way we can accept the command to "pray constantly" as referring to a real possibility is by saying that the entire life of the saint taken as a whole is a single great prayer. What is customarily called prayer is, then, a part of this prayer. Now prayer in the ordinary sense ought to be made no less than three times each day. This is evident from the story of Daniel, who prayed three times a day when such great peril had been devised for him. And Peter went up to the housetop about the sixth hour to pray; that is when he saw the sheet descending from heaven let down by four corners. He was offering the middle prayer of the three, the one referred to before him by David, "In the morning may you hear…

Thus we possess other hands, of which it is said: "The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice." For if I lift up these hands of mine, while the hands of my soul remain hanging down, and not raised to holy and good deeds, then the lifting up of my hands will not be an evening sacrifice.

"I was struck dumb and did not open my mouth, because it is you who did it". This too we have already expounded above, when we treated that verse which says: "While the sinner stands against me, I was struck dumb and was humbled and kept silence from good things". For it is good that at the time when weapons—whether of disparagements, or of insults, or of reproaches—are hurled against us, we should remember this verse which says: "I was struck dumb and did not open my mouth, because it is you who did it". This indeed seems to need inquiry: what is it that he said, "It is you who did it", and yet did not add what he did. But the very order teaches us, since it describes as a kind of contest between us and the sinner who stands against us; and that it indicates that God did this very thing, that is, that for the sake of our exercise and progress God made these struggles. Therefore for…

The ultimate justice itself is Christ, "who was made wisdom for us from God, and justice, and sanctification and redemption." The justice in each person, however, is formed from that justice, so that many justices come into existence in those who are saved; wherefore it has also been written, "The Lord is just and has loved justice."
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6:40

quotes.quote:
Amen I say to you, that this generation shall not pass away, until all these things be done. Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.

Let us see what this generation is, of which Christ speaks.

And the simple, indeed, refer these words to the destruction of Jerusalem; and they suppose it was said of that generation which existed in the time of Christ and looked upon his suffering, a generation that would not pass away before the destruction of that city came to pass.

But I do not know whether they can expound word for word what he says: "do you not see all these things? amen I say to you, there shall not be left here one stone upon another that shall not be destroyed" down to that which he says: it is near, at the door. For perhaps in some points they will be able, but in others they will not be able at all, and, sufficiently hemmed in, I do not know…

It is said of God in the eighteenth psalm that "God made darkness his hiding place." This is a Hebrew way of showing that the ideas of God that people understand in accordance with their merits are obscure and unknowable, since God hides himself as if in darkness from those who cannot bear the radiance of the knowledge of him and who cannot see him, partly because of the defilement of the mind that is bound to a human "body of humiliation," partly because of its restricted capacity to comprehend God.… Moreover, our Savior and Lord, the Logos of God, shows the depth of the knowledge of the Father, and that, although a derived knowledge is possessed by those whose minds are illuminated by the divine Logos himself, absolute understanding and knowledge of the Father is possessed by himself alone in accordance with his merits, when he says, "No one has known the Son save the Father, and no…

The reasons of the divine dispensation and providence are most obscure. For "God made darkness his hiding place." Those desiring audaciously and rashly to examine this darkness and appropriating for themselves one thing from another have fallen headlong into the dense "darkness" of errors.

But since we sin most of all at that time, when the sinner stands against us, instigating and provoking us to send forth from our mouth something such as would hold us guilty in the future judgment, the holy Prophet, describing this, says: "While the sinner stood against me, I was dumb and was humbled and kept silence from good things". Whenever the sinner stood against me and spoke ill of me, and disparaged and irritated me to render him the like, and to bring forth from my mouth things equal to his, I at that time meditated silence, so as to answer nothing at all. Therefore he says: "While the sinner stood against me, I was dumb and was humbled and kept silence from good things". But we sometimes, if we are unwilling to be humbled, think other things and say within ourselves: What is this? This man has held me in contempt and has dared to thrust such things in my face, and thus to…

And what did he add to these things? "And my sorrow", he says, "was renewed". Those who in the struggle of the contest engage in mutual blows against one another always try to prepare themselves in these things, so that they may bravely bear the blows inflicted on them by their adversaries, and not receive the sense of pain, and this is for them the highest excellence: to sustain the strokes of arms or of heels without pain. Among these, that man is more perfect who, at the stroke of the wound, receives no sting of pain. But the second is he who indeed feels pain, but by no means yields to the pains. Understand something of this sort also in ourselves, when we are cursed, and the antagonist stands against us; if indeed we are well instructed, and strengthened in mind by long meditation, we are in no way at all grieved by the curses or reproaches inflicted, but by reason of the exceeding…

Therefore "my neighbors stood afar off, and they who sought my soul did violence. And they who sought evils for me spoke vanity". These things again he says of others. For there are certain men who seek evils for the righteous, and do not rejoice so much when they hear something of his good deeds as they take glad congratulation when they hear evils, and, as it were, exult when they see the righteous man in some evils. And these are they who, when they have seen the righteous man confessing his sins, vomit out, as it were, some harmful venom; on account of which he says: "And they who sought my soul did violence. And they who sought evils for me spoke vanities". And truly it is most manifestly perceived that not only those who seek evils for the righteous, but everyone who tries to inflict evils upon anyone whatever, speaks vanity. For he who seeks to do evils does not speak those…

"They, therefore, who sought evils for me spoke vanities, and meditated deceit all the day long". See the one who lies in ambush for the righteous. For I already call righteous the one who becomes "his own accuser in the first place", as the word of Scripture indicates. For just as Scripture calls that man wise who, when he is reproved, does not hate the one who reproves him, but rather loves him: so also he is called righteous who, after his transgression, does not persist in his transgressions, nor awaits that the devil become his accuser, nor that the devil bring his sins forward into the midst, but himself reproves and convicts himself, and through his confession is freed from death. For "they who sought evils for me spoke vanity, and meditated deceit all the day long. But I, as though deaf, did not hear". Nothing more excellent than this virtue, nothing more surpassing, can be…

There are those who take up the testament of God through their mouth and, though they have the law of God in their mouth, their life and their acts differ far from their words and discourses; "for they say and do not". Concerning whom the prophet too says: "but to the sinner God said: why do you declare my justices, and take up my testament through your mouth?". You see, then, how this one ruminates, who has the testament of God in his mouth. But what is said to him in what follows? "But you have hated discipline, and cast my words behind you". In which it plainly shows this one indeed to be "ruminating", but "not dividing the hoof", and therefore whoever is such is unclean.

Yet this leper is commanded to cover only his "mouth": what is this, that he is enjoined to have all the parts of the body naked, and only the "mouth" he is commanded to cover? Is it not plain and set in the open that to him who is in the leprosy of sin speech is closed, the "mouth" is closed to him, so that the confidence of speech and the authority of teaching are shut out? For "to the sinner God said: Why dost thou declare my righteous acts, and takest up my covenant through thy mouth?" Let the sinner, then, have his "mouth" closed, because he who has not taught himself cannot teach another; and therefore he who by acting evilly has lost the freedom of speaking is commanded to cover his "mouth."

He takes up a testimony and interprets of Christ that which was written not of Christ, but of the saints generally. For freely and with all confidence I contradict the devil, that this cannot be understood of the person of Christ. For he does not need the help of the angels, who is greater than the angels and has obtained by inheritance a name better than they. To none of the angels did God ever say: "You are my Son, this day have I begotten you." To none of them did he speak as to a son, "he who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire," but to his own proper Son, of whom he speaks innumerable things in the prophets. He does not need, I say, the help of the angels, the Son of God. But that you may know that you have interpreted wrongly, and that what follows is to be understood not of Christ but of the saints, listen. "From ruin and the noonday demon" God delivers not…

quotes.quote: By these words he seems to teach that anyone lying on his bed ought to seek the reason within himself for those things that he has done throughout the day, and in light of those acts he has done against reason he ought to expose them and disapprove of them and feel their sting, for if this is done correctly from his bed he will not be drawn away from honest deeds.

Certainly, people place their glory in various places, some in their country, some in family line, some in beauty, some in the strength of their bodies and in their skill of competing in the contest, being very elated they have overcome these people or those by their physical struggling. And why is it necessary to recount all the things through which those unknown gods are glorified, "whose glory is in their shame," as the apostle said? God is the glory of the saint who trusts him, glory, I say, not blindly credited but credited through faith that is reckoned as righteousness, through which one is enabled to see the signs of a present God and participate in his strength. So, God was the glory of Moses who loved the prophet so much that he revealed himself to the point of showing his face both before all the Hebrew people and before the Egyptians. God was the glory of the prophet Elijah,…

We readily accept this psalm as spoken from the person of David, as we have noted in its title. According to history, certain men were hurting David, many of whom as their number increased were joining themselves to Absalom.… Those who were oppressing the Savior were Jews who were shouting, "Away with him; away with him!" Judas the betrayer and Caiphas rose up against him. The ones who said that there was no deliverance of his life were the same ones passing by him at the time of his suffering who said, "Come down from the cross and we will believe you." … But, one may also understand this passage in this way: all the rulers and teachers of subjects that are foreign to the decrees of Christ who have come against him. The people who cling to them and follow their teaching cause him trial. Finally, they who, neither teaching contrary matters nor instructed by false teaching, believe that…

But after these things he added a certain mystical saying, which is beyond my hearing, and above my tongue, which exceeds my understanding. For he says, whether concerning all sinners, or concerning some one sinner — for he speaks in the singular: "Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be". He says that there is indeed a little while yet from the present time up to the consummation of the age, or perhaps even beyond the consummation of the age, and until that avenging fire consume the adversaries. But if this comes to pass in some manner, the sinner shall not be; and by what reasoning it can come to pass that he be not a sinner, let him examine and inquire who can. "Yet a little while, and the sinner shall not be, and you shall seek his place and not find it". But not only shall the sinner not be, but neither shall there be a place of the sinner. And what is the place of the…

"By the Lord", he says, "are the steps of a man directed". And elsewhere in this psalm he speaks of the steps of the righteous man in this way: "The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps shall not be supplanted". But also in the seventy-second psalm it is said: "My steps had almost been poured out". We therefore name "steps" (gressus) from "walking" (gradiendo), according to that which is written in Exodus, that Moses saw a flame of fire and an angel, when the bush indeed burned but was not consumed, and he said: "Stepping aside, or passing over, I will behold this great vision". From this passage, then, an occasion is given us for understanding the things we have in hand. Therefore concerning those things which we have recalled as written in Exodus — that is, "stepping aside I will behold this great vision" — I heard a certain one of the wise men before us saying, when he was…

If you wish to explain what it is to hope in everything, we are going to say that it is nothing other than to become an heir of the kingdom of heaven, to receive comfort, to be called the children of God, to see God, to be satisfied by the righteousness for which one hungers and thirsts, to enjoy his abundant mercy and to live in all the things which the true God and our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ promised.

"Because those who bless him shall inherit the earth; but those who curse him shall be exterminated". Those who bless him, that is, those who bless the righteous, shall inherit the earth. Which earth?—that good earth, that abundant earth, that earth flowing with milk and honey, where are those good things which are truly good; that they shall possess who bless the righteous, but those who curse him shall be exterminated. And to you it sometimes seems a small thing to speak evil of the saints, and it is very light for you to say of the servants of God, "That one is such and such, that one dissembles, and that one loves the world, but that one is an impostor"—do you not hear that those who curse the righteous shall be exterminated? Or if this seems small to you, hear elsewhere God saying to the righteous: "I will be an enemy to your enemies, and I will oppose your adversaries". You see…

"Remove your plagues from me; from the strength of your hand I have fainted". What the Latin translators rendered "plagues," in the Greek codices is written "scourges," so that it is: "Remove your scourges from me". This one seems, of course, to say when he is set as it were under the correction of scourges, when, like a man, he is corrected for his sins, or scourged that he may be amended. Just as that also is understood by very many which is written: "Son, do not grow weary of the discipline of God, nor faint when you are rebuked by him. For whom God loves, he corrects, and scourges every son whom he receives". Whenever, therefore, anyone is rebuked with corrections of this kind, he seems fittingly to say: "Remove your scourges from me. From the strength of your hand I have fainted". But that also seems fittingly to be applied which is written: "In rebukes on account of iniquity you…

Indeed, in the same way the rays of the sun touch the face of one who looks at it, and in fact it is impossible for one who stands near to the sun not to feel it, so also it must be understood that the individual who is fully a partaker of God is the one who has meditated on the law of the holy word and who has surrendered his mind to understanding God. Which, I believe, the prophet indicates in this place when he says, "The light of your countenance is manifested toward us, O Lord." The representation of the light that shines in your countenance is imprinted on us as it comes to us, and that very light is the expression of your countenance, so that one who is able to see the sign of the divine light that is manifested, immediately recognizes that God's light is made in us. I think that this mystery is also declared in Exodus when the face of Moses, as he is speaking intimately with…

"But the meek shall inherit the earth". Against the Valentinians and the other heretics, who think that my Savior says in the Gospel things which are not in the ancient Writings, this verse is to be brought forward, just as we too have learned from a certain presbyter to bring these things forward for the convincing of them. For what was said in the Gospel: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth", see how it was already said before by the Holy Spirit through David: nay, Christ himself now says in the Gospels: "Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth by inheritance". The Prophet indeed adds even something more than we read in the Gospel, saying: "And they shall delight in the multitude of peace". Here too the Greek uses that very word of which we spoke above also, κατατρυφήσουσιν, that is, they shall take delight rather than they shall be delighted.…
And what does sin smell of? Concerning this the prophet says the following: "My wounds stink and fester because of my folly."

These are they who can also say what follows: "for my scars have festered and rotted." "Do not," says the Savior, "cast your pearls before swine," there calling swine those who take delight in the stenches of their sins, who seek out every stench as a most sweet odor. Consider, then, the sinner who takes delight in his sins and is glad in his evils: since he too wallows in stinking dung, and perceives no feeling of his own stench, which is given off from the dung of sin, but takes delight as though in the highest pleasures and most pleasing delights. But if it should happen to this man at some time to lay aside the sense and smell of swine and to receive the sense of the word of God, so that he can feel the stench of his own sins: immediately, turned to repentance and seeking amendment, he becomes impatient of his own stench, crying out to the heavenly physician, and, showing the scars…

Now among the Greeks I know there was only one Phaedon, not a second, and one Polemon, who devoted themselves to philosophy, after a licentious and most wicked life. However, with Jesus there were not only at the time we are speaking of, the twelve disciples, but many more at all times, who, becoming a band of temperate people, speak in the following way of their former lives: "For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But after that the kindness and love of God our Savior toward humankind appeared, by the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, which he shed on us richly," we became such as we are. For "God sent forth his Word and healed them and delivered them from their destructions," as the prophet taught in the book of Psalms.

Becoming confused by his efforts to accuse us, Celsus contradicts himself, appearing at one time to know a person "without sin" and "a righteous individual who can look up to God [adorned] with virtue from the beginning." At another time he accepts our statement that there is no human being who is altogether righteous or without sin. He seems to admit this truth when he remarks, "This is indeed apparently true, that somehow the human race is naturally inclined to sin." In the next place, as if all people were not invited by the word, he says, "All people, then, without distinction, ought to be invited, since all indeed are sinners." And yet, in the preceding pages, we have pointed out the words of Jesus: "Come to me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." All people, therefore, laboring and being heavily burdened on account of the nature of sin, are invited to…
We will have to say that if we give in to troubles, we do not believe in him insofar as he is endurance; and if we are weak, we have not believed in him insofar as he is strength.

quotes.quote: There follows: "And now what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord?" As Christ is our wisdom, and Christ is righteousness, according to what is written: "Who was made wisdom for us from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption"; so also our expectation, that is, our patience, is Christ. Therefore let not the wise man glory in wisdom, nor the strong in his strength, because we have all things in Christ. And now therefore what is my expectation, that is, my patience? The Lord. "And my substance is from you". If I have a substance of spiritual riches, it is from God; "for God breathed into the face of man the breath of life, and man was made into a living soul".

"My flesh will rest in hope." The Lord Jesus Christ says these words, whose flesh is the first to rest in hope. Crucified, made the first fruit of the dead and having been taken into heaven after the resurrection, he carried the earthly body with him so that even the heavenly powers were awestruck and terrified seeing the flesh ascending into heaven. Concerning Elijah it was written that he was taken up into heaven; and about Enoch, that he was translated. Now, however, it is said that Jesus ascended into heaven. Let him be offended who so wishes at our word. I, however, guard it will all faith because just as Christ is the first fruit from the dead, so also he is the first to carry his flesh to heaven.

Those therefore who on this account are troubled and anxious, God will be their protector in the time of tribulation, in the time of judgment, when the impious shall be delivered to punishments: then the Lord will both help them in the time of tribulation, and deliver them, and take them away from sinners — not only from sinful men, but also from the contrary powers, or certainly at that time when the soul is separated from the body, and there meet it the sinful demons, the adverse powers, the spirits of this air, who wish to detain it and recall it to themselves if they shall have recognized in it anything of their own works and deeds. For to each soul as it goes forth from this world there comes the prince of this world, and the aerial powers, and they inquire whether they may find in it anything of their own; if they shall have found avarice, it belongs to their part; if wrath, if…

There is a sleep which the disciples are commanded to sleep with rest, according to Christ's command, differing greatly from a sleeping against his will; so that the order might be preserved: that first indeed we should watch, praying that we may not enter into temptation, and afterward that we should sleep and rest according to Christ's command.

Which sleep Solomon too sets down in a promise to those who live well, saying in his Proverbs: "for if you sit down, you will be without fear; but if you sleep, you will sleep sweetly, and you will not fear a terror that comes upon you nor the assaults of the impious rushing in". And David, knowing the diverse watchings and sleepings, "swore to the Lord and vowed a vow to the God of Jacob": not to go up onto the couch of his bed nor to give sleep to his eyes nor slumber to his eyelids, and to do this for so long, until he should find "a place…

"For I am ready for scourges". This too is the voice of a good and, so to speak, excellent sinner, who has indeed transgressed, yet awaits the scourges of his transgressions, by which he wishes to be amended in the present, lest he be punished and perish in the future. Set before your eyes a sinner saying to the Lord: I, because I have sinned, am even now ready for scourges; do not reserve me for eternal fire, do not reserve me for the outer darkness. While I am in this life, requite me for my sins, since You scourge every son whom You receive. I beseech You, scourge me too, and do not reserve me with those who are not scourged, who "are not in the labors of men, and shall not be scourged with men", that is, who are utterly forsaken by You, whose amendment and correction You do not seek. Knowing, therefore, what difference there is when a sinner is scourged by Him who "scourges every…

But lest we tarry too long over the several kinds of the virtues, we can briefly say that by these things are signified those with which the Church is adorned. Her faith can be compared to gold; the word of preaching to silver, the brass to patience; to the incorruptible woods, the knowledge which comes through the wood, or the incorruption of chastity, which never grows old; to the fine linen, virginity; to the scarlet, the glory of confession; to the purple, the splendor of charity; to the hyacinth, the hope of the kingdom of heaven. Let these for the present be the materials out of which the whole tabernacle is constructed, the priests are clothed, and the high priest also is adorned. And what their garments are, or of what sort, the prophet declares in another place and says: "Let thy priests be clothed with righteousness"; all these, then, are garments of righteousness. And again…

[The blessed person] meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, not as one who entrusts the words of the law to his memory without works, but as one who by meditating performs works consistent with it, until through the disciplined meditation of the works that the law instructs, he is prepared for excelling in all the things that apply for living perfectly according to the law.

Certainly, even if I shall not have been able to understand everything, if I am, nevertheless, busily engaged in the divine Scriptures and "I meditate on the law of God day and night" and at no time at all do I desist inquiring, discussing, investigating, and certainly, what is greatest, praying God and asking for understanding from him who "teaches humankind knowledge," I shall appear to dwell "at the well of vision." … You too, therefore, if you shall always search the prophetic visions, if you always inquire, always desire to learn, if you meditate on these things, if you remain in them, you too will receive a blessing from the Lord and dwell "at the well of vision." For the Lord Jesus will appear to you also, "in the way," and will open the Scriptures to you so that you may say, "Was not our heart burning within us when he opened to us the Scriptures?" But he appears to those who…

Therefore on this account we are enlightened by the commandment of the Lord, so that, when the flame of unlawful jealousy has beaten upon our heart and mind, we, taught by the words, may say: If I should wish to be jealous among the malignant, or should envy those who work iniquity, see what follows: "Like grass", he says, "they shall quickly wither, and like the green herbs they shall quickly fall away". Do you wish also to be fortified by the authority of another prophet's admonitions concerning such men? Hear what Isaiah too pronounces concerning all carnal glory: "All flesh", he says, "is grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass". Do you wish also to see through particular cases how the glory of the flesh is the flower of grass? See who ruled thirty years ago, how his rule flowered: but straightway like the flower of grass it withered; then afterward another after him, then…

Whence the Savior himself speaks: "but I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people". He saw in his mother's womb the uncleanness of bodies; walled about on this side and that by her inward parts, he endured the confinements of earthly dregs; whence he likens himself to a worm and says: "I am a worm and not a man". For man is wont to be born of male and female, but I was born not of male and female, according to the rite and nature of men, but after the pattern of the "worm", whose seed is not from elsewhere, but whose origin is in the very bodies, and from the very bodies, in which it grows together.

quotes.quote: "The Lord knows the days of the spotless, and their inheritance shall be forever". According to the Scriptures, as we have observed in many places, the Lord does not know all things, but only those that are good; but he is said to be ignorant of evils, not that there is truly anything that lies hidden from his knowledge, but those things which are unworthy of his notice, he is said to be ignorant of. Which we have also shown from the Scriptures, when the Apostle says: "If anyone among you be a prophet, or spiritual, let him know the things that I write to you, that they are the Lord's". But if anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored. And in the Gospel, where the Lord says to sinners: "I know you not, depart from me, workers of iniquity". For just as it is said elsewhere: "The Lord knows who are his"; so here the Lord is said to know not the days of the impious, but of the spotless. For…

God is ignorant of evil deeds, not because he is unable to understand everything or to grasp it with his own intelligence (for it is wrong to think this way about God) but because those deeds are unworthy of his contemplation.… God is ignorant of the way of the wicked, and he knows the way of the righteous. Further, who is the way of the righteous except the one who said, "I am the way" whom the Father knows? "No one has known the Son except the Father." The distinction between the knowledge and ignorance of God is referred to in the prophets as "the memory and forgetfulness" of God. Often it is said in prayer: "Be mindful of me" and "Why have you forgotten our poverty?" Just as God removes sinners from his own memory, so does he again receive the repentant and become mindful of them.

At every single reading, "when Moses is read," we must pray to the Father of the Word, that He may fulfill even in us that which is written in the Psalms: "unveil my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law." For unless He Himself opens our eyes, how shall we be able to see these so great mysteries that are shaped in the Patriarchs, which are figured now in wells, now in marriages, now in childbearings, now even in barrennesses?

Let us therefore, we too, if it is thus necessary, fall into your detractions, provided only that the Church, now turned to Christ the Lord, may know the truth of the Word of God covered under the covering of the letter; for so the Apostle also said, that: "if anyone shall be turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away; for where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." Therefore the Lord himself, the Holy Spirit himself, must be entreated by us, that he may deign to take away every mist and every darkness which, thickened by the filth of sins, obscures the sight of our heart, so that we may be able to contemplate the spiritual and wonderful understanding of his law, according to him who said: "Uncover my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law."

The eyes of our inner man see with greater clarity: "Open my eyes, and I shall see the wonders of Thy law." Does this mean that his eyes were covered with a veil? No. But our eyes are our mind. To Jesus alone it belongs to remove this veil, so that we may be able to understand the Scripture and to grasp what is obscurely expressed.

When we fail to remember the one who formed each one of us in the womb, and formed all our hearts individually and understands all our works, we do not perceive that God is a helper of those who are lowly and inferior, a protector of the weak, a shelterer of those who have been given up in despair and Savior of those who have been given up as hopeless.

quotes.quote: "When the sinners shall have perished, you shall see". Perhaps this will be first, that the righteous may see the sinners and the impious condemned. For to sinners first are decreed penalties and punishments: and when the righteous shall have seen these, and shall have recognized what difference there is between a good life and an evil one, and shall have understood from what great evils they have escaped by living well — so that those who are in punishments, seeing them in glory, say: "We fools thought their life madness" — after therefore they shall have seen how the sinners perish, then they themselves shall be exalted and borne up to heaven that they may inherit the earth. Now the word admonishes and applies a solace to this matter which frequently enough beats upon the heart of almost all men. For, because frequently we who are weak, seeing certain wicked and impious men passing…

Let us come, if you will, also to the circumcision of the lips. I think that he is "uncircumcised in lips" who has not yet ceased from foolish speech, from scurrility, who disparages good men, who accuses his neighbors, who instigates quarrels, who stirs up slanders, who sets brothers against one another by speaking falsehoods, who utters vain, foolish, worldly, unchaste, base, injurious, insolent, blasphemous things and the rest which are unworthy of a Christian. But if anyone restrains his mouth from all these, and "orders his words in judgment," represses verbosity, tempers his tongue, moderates his words, he is deservedly said to be circumcised in lips. But also "those who speak iniquity on high and stretch their tongue up to heaven," as the heretics do, are to be called uncircumcised and unclean in lips, whereas he is circumcised and clean who always speaks the word of God and sets…
It is not possible to know him if one has not become still and purified one's mind.

quotes.quote: Yet I remember that some time ago, when we were expounding that verse of the hundred and eighteenth psalm in which it is written: "your law is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths", we showed, according to our ability, the difference between the "lamp" and the "light". For we said that he assigned the "lamp" indeed to the "feet", that is, to the lower parts of the body, but gave the "light" to the "paths", which "paths" in another place are called "eternal paths". Since, then, according to a certain mystical meaning, this world is understood as the lower parts of creation, therefore the "lamp" of the law is recorded as kindled for those who are in this world as it were the feet of the whole creation. But the "light" will be eternal for those "paths" along which in the age to come each one will walk according to his merits.

His next remark was, "Have not these inferior powers had assigned to them by God different departments, according as each was deemed worthy?" But this is a question which requires a very profound knowledge. For we must determine whether the Word of God, who governs all things, has appointed wicked demons for certain employments, in the same way as in states executioners are appointed, and other officers with cruel but needful duties to discharge; or whether as among robbers, who infest desert places, it is customary for them to choose out of their number one who may be their leader,—so the demons, who are scattered as it were in troops in different parts of the earth, have chosen for themselves a chief under whose command they may plunder and pillage the souls of men. To explain this fully, and to justify the conduct of the Christians in refusing homage to any object except the Most…

However, we must know that Psalm 68 [LXX], which contains the statement, "The zeal of your house has devoured me," and a little later "They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink," both having been recorded in the Gospels, is placed in the mouth of Christ, indicating no change in the person of the speaker.

quotes.quote: And immediately one of them ran up, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink. And thus he fulfilled in himself the prophecy that spoke of him: "and they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink". For this reason too, according to John, when Jesus had received the vinegar with the gall, he said: "it is finished" — this also, which the Scripture had foretold concerning me. And one may with pleasure apply this text against those who have written or do write malicious things against Christ, of whom Isaiah says: "woe to those who write malicious things; for in writing they write malicious things" (I speak of those who have left behind certain writings, speaking "iniquity on high"). And one will use this text when he sees them gathering from certain things they have heard — whether of heathen sayings or of barbarous…

From what stones? He was certainly not pointing to irrational and bodily stones, but to insensible men, once hard, who, because they worshiped stones or wood, had that fulfilled in them which was sung in the psalm concerning such men: "let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them". Truly those who make idols and trust in them are like their gods: they have been turned, without sense and without any reason, into stones and wood. For although they see so great an order of created things, their beauty, their function, so great a beauty of the world, they are unwilling to understand the creator from the created things, nor do they consider that there is some providence over so great a dispensation, some governor; but they are blind, seeing the world only with those eyes with which irrational beasts of burden and wild animals see. For they do not perceive that there is…

quotes.quote: If the meditation is wisdom, what will the message be? When the meditation of the heart is wisdom, wicked thoughts will not come within it, nor is a place given to the devil or those things that defile people.

Clearly sins are said to be the death of the soul, from the phrase and you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins. And since 'trespass' is a term proper to Scripture, we must examine whether it differs from 'sin,' especially since here it is said in combination: and you, being dead in your trespasses and your sins. And we inquire whether the things already wickedly accomplished by us are called our 'sins,' while the beginnings of these—being, as it were, not yet falls, but on their way toward our actually falling—are 'trespasses.' And perhaps for this reason it is said in the eighteenth Psalm, "Who shall understand trespasses?", because the one who understands the roots and beginnings of sins, which are 'trespasses,' would be able also to guard himself against falling into 'sins' as well.

I think that the discourse, wishing to show a general cleanness which is not only in acts but also in knowledge, says in the twenty-third Psalm: who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? he that is innocent in hands and pure in heart, and in the Proverbs: who shall boast that he has a chaste heart? or who shall be confident that he is clean from sins? I therefore think that the one clean in heart and chaste in heart is no other than he who possesses a heart clean and chaste from every false dogma; so also I reckon him to be innocent in hands and clean from sins who is irreproachable in the acts of his life. And it must be known that (as regards the truth) it is impossible for anyone to be innocent in hands and clean from sins without being pure in heart and chaste from false dogmas; just as, on the contrary, it is impossible to be clean indeed…

Just as one man advances according to God, and by applying zeal to himself becomes better than his former self, so also it used to happen to the whole people. And on this account, as it too advanced, there came to it also an increase of the law. In short, just as it is written in the law, there are certain precepts for the priests and Levites concerning sacrifices and the other solemn observances: yet when the people advanced, at that time when there was still in it the power of advancing, the matter did not stand still in that first order, but there were bound to those men certain more eminent legislations, a second and a third. And if anyone wishes to know what these things are that were added concerning the priests and Levites, let him read the first book of Chronicles, and let him patiently examine that whole catalogue of names, and he will find there a certain admirable order and a…

But now let us at last see what the voice of the righteous man utters, and, seeing ourselves as though in a mirror, let us look at ourselves, whether we can be such, or whether much is lacking to us, or whether indeed we are now near, although we have not yet fully attained. Since therefore the beginning of many sins is human speech, and our mouth serves many evils, and it is very difficult to find a man who, for even one hour at least, keeps his mouth and his tongue from sin, he says: "I said: I will keep my ways, that I sin not with my tongue". I said to my very self, and I spoke within myself, and I added these things: Thus I wish to keep my ways, that I sin not; in this way I can keep them, if I guard my tongue. "For by thy words", he says, "thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned". And again: "Amen I say to you, for every idle word you shall render an…

Celsus, … as one who has heard the subject of humility greatly talked about but who has not been at pains to understand it, would wish to speak evil of that humility that is practiced among us, and imagines that it is borrowed from some words of Plato imperfectly understood, where he expresses himself in the Laws as follows: "Now God, according to the ancient account, having in himself both the beginning and end and middle of all existing things, proceeds according to nature and marches straight on. He is constantly followed by justice, which is the avenger of all breaches of the divine law: he who is about to become happy follows [justice] closely in humility, and becomingly adorned." He did not observe, however, that in writers much older than Plato the following words occur in a prayer: "Lord, my heart is not haughty or my eyes lofty, neither do I walk in great matters, nor in things…

Let Celsus then say distinctly that the great diversity among the products of the earth is not the work of Providence but that a certain fortuitous concurrence of atoms gave birth to qualities so diverse, and that it was owing to chance that so many kinds of plants and trees and herbs resemble one another, and that no disposing reason gave existence to them, and that they do not derive their origin from an understanding that is beyond all admiration. We Christians, however, who are devoted to the worship of the only God, who created these things, feel grateful for them to him who made them, because not only for us but also (on our account) for the animals that are subject to us, he has prepared such a home, seeing "he causes the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of humans, that they may bring forth food out of the earth and wine that makes glad the heart of people,…

See the greatness of the Lord: "into all the earth has the sound of his teaching gone out, and his words unto the ends of the world". Our Lord Jesus, because he is the power of God, has been poured out over the whole world, and at the present moment is with us according to that which is read in the Apostle: "when you are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of the Lord Jesus". The power of the Lord and Savior is both with those who are separated from our world in Britain, and with those in Mauritania, and with all who under the sun have believed in his name. See, then, the greatness of the Savior, how it has been poured out over the whole world — and certainly I have not yet set forth his true greatness.

quotes.quote: Do not seek on earth that "oil" which is poured "upon the head" of the "great priest" that he may become Christ; but if it seems good, learn from the prophet David what this "oil" is: "you have loved" he says "righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows". This, then, is the "oil of gladness" which, "poured upon his head", made him Christ.

"The sinner shall watch the righteous, and shall gnash upon him with his teeth". For just as by nature light and darkness are contrary, so contrary to one another are the sinner and the righteous. And if you see the righteous man at any time held in hatred, do not hesitate to say of him who hates the righteous, that he is a sinner. If you see him who lives well suffering persecution, do not hesitate to say of him who persecutes, that he is not only a sinner, but wicked. The sinner, therefore, shall watch the righteous, and watching him shall gnash upon him with his teeth. As for what he says, "he shall gnash with his teeth", I know not whether it is to be taken of bodily teeth, although it be possible that this too be done by the sinner against the righteous. When he threatens him, when he rages against him, when he is silent in voice, and cries out in fury, when he contrives snares for…

This is doubtless what David too says in the Psalms: "let his prayer become sin", when not only nothing of merit, but even much of guilt is sought from the sacrifices. For you hear the lawgiver decree that, if anyone eats of that "which has remained over to the third day, he shall bear the sin". Whence it is to be recognized how great a stain of sins threatens the human condition, since sin arises even from that place where the victim of propitiation is offered.

In the Psalms the prophet gives thanks saying, "He who lifts me up from the gates of death that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion." And from this we learn that it is never possible for anyone to be fit to declare the praises of God, unless he has been lifted up from the gates of death and has come to the gates of Zion.

quotes.quote: Even if one turns to the lesser fragments of the body, one can discover their incorporeal correspondences in the soul. "… Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are shaken." What bones of the prophet were shaken? The harmonious state of his soul and the strength of his mind were shattered, and therefore he asks God for the restoration of his bones.

"For I said: Lest my enemies ever insult over me". When I was charged, and did not return like for like to those who charged me, I said these things: "If I have repaid those who requited me with evils", I shall assuredly be forsaken by God, and, forsaken, I must needs fall. And when I have fallen, my enemies will insult over me. But if I do not repay evils for evils, but leave the judgment to God, aided by Him I shall not fall down, but shall stand firmly, and my enemies will not insult over me. I also said this: "While my feet were being moved, they spoke great things against me". As long as I stand undismayed and unmoved, my enemies will not speak great things against me, for they have nothing to say. But as soon as I waver — I will not say, fall — at once they will begin to reproach and to say: Do you see this man? Behold, what has he himself done! And while he teaches these things,…

But the things said in this passage can also be understood otherwise, more plainly. For many people think, when they look upon the creatures and contemplate this world, that they see them. And why do I speak of people? Behold, the birds and the four-footed beasts see the sun and the moon and the whole heaven together with the choir of stars, but they do not understand their reasons; only the just and holy, comprehending them through the reason of the wisdom of God, look upon them. Therefore in the eighth Psalm David says: "for I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have founded". For does the prophet not now "see the heaven and the moon"? But this, that he says: "I shall see", if we consider it, we shall be able to understand.

But the angels also are called spirits and fire: "he who makes", it says, "his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire"; to the holy ones they are spirits, but to those who deserve punishments they supply fire and burning. According to which sense our Lord and Savior too, since he is "spirit", "came to send fire upon the earth".

quotes.quote: And the holy Scriptures bear witness to the Gospel announcements made by the Apostles and to that made by our Saviour. David says of the Apostles, perhaps also of the evangelists: "The Lord shall give the word to those that preach with great power; the King of the powers of the beloved;" teaching at the same time that it is not skilfully composed discourse, nor the mode of delivery, nor well practised eloquence that produces conviction, but the communication of divine power. Hence also Paul says: "I will know not the word that is puffed up, but the power; for the kingdom of God is not in word but in power." And in another passage: "And my word and my preaching were not persuasive words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the spirit and of power." To this power Simon and Cleophas bear witness when they say: "Was not our heart burning within us by the way, as he opened to us the…
