quotes.quote: For the word of God declares that the preaching (although in itself true and most worthy of belief) is not sufficient to reach the human heart, unless a certain power be imparted to the speaker from God, and a grace appear upon his words; and it is only by the divine agency that this takes place in those who speak effectually. The prophet says in the Psalms 67, that "the Lord will give a word with great power to them who preach." If, then, it should be granted with respect to certain points, that the same doctrines are found among the Greeks as in our own Scriptures, yet they do not possess the same power of attracting and disposing the souls of men to follow them. And therefore the disciples of Jesus, men ignorant so far as regards Grecian philosophy, yet traversed many countries of the world, impressing, agreeably to the desire of the Logos, each one of their hearers according to his…

"All my bones will say: 'Lord, who is like Thee?'" Behold, bones that chatter, reason, hold forth, feel God — and this despite the insensitivity to which the physicians testify who saw through the bones of a patient, without his feeling anything under the action of the saw. "All my bones will say: 'Lord, who is like Thee?'" It is precisely the inner man who possesses all these bones.

But when "bones shall have been joined to bones and joints to joints", according to what we said above, then he himself too will say of us that prophetic word: "all my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?". For "all" these "bones" speak and utter a hymn and give thanks to God. For they remember his benefit, and therefore "all my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you? delivering the poor man from the hand of one stronger than he". Of these bones, while they were still scattered, before he came who was to "collect and gather them into one", that prophetic word too was spoken: "our bones are scattered beside hell". Because, then, they were scattered, therefore he says through another prophet: "let bone be gathered to bone and joint to joint and sinews and veins and skins". For when this shall have been done, then "all these shall say: Lord, who is like you? delivering the needy from…

This cup of the passion which is drunk Scripture names in many places, especially that which is properly drunk by the martyrs, as it is there: "what shall I render to the Lord for all the things which he has rendered to me? I will receive the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord". If therefore the cup of salvation is the cup of martyrdom, it is necessary that we preserve that cup, drinking the whole of it, because it is the cup of salvation, so that we pour out nothing of it. He therefore drinks the whole cup who suffers for the testimony whatever shall have been brought upon him; but he pours it out as he receives it who, called to martyrdom, denies lest he suffer anything. There is also another kind of "inebriating cup", which one drinks after he shall have eaten the "table" prepared for him by God "against those who trouble" the just man.

And again in the fourteenth Psalm he says: "Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle? or who shall rest in thy holy mountain? He that entereth without spot and worketh righteousness" and the rest. Or indeed how will it be true that it is said of this tabernacle that none dwells in it except the "innocent in hands and clean in heart, who hath not taken his soul in vain", when the history of the Kingdoms discloses that most wicked priests, "sons of pestilence", dwelt in the tabernacle of God, and that the very ark of the testament, captured by the Allophyli (Philistines), was held among the impious and profane? From all which it stands firm that the prophet thinks with a far other sense concerning this tabernacle, in which he says that none dwells except the "innocent in hands and clean in heart, and who hath not taken his soul in vain, nor done evil to his neighbor, and hath not received…

But what does it profit me, if the seed of Abraham, "which is Christ," should possess "the cities of his enemies for an inheritance" and should not possess my city? If in my city, that is, in my soul, which is "the city of the great king," neither his laws nor his ordinances should be observed? What does it profit me that he has subjected the whole world and possesses the cities of his enemies if he should not also conquer his enemies in me, if he should not destroy "the law that is in my members fighting against the law of my mind and that leads me captive in the law of sin"? So, therefore, let each one of us do what is necessary that Christ may also conquer the enemies in his soul and in his body, and, subjecting and triumphing over them, may possess the city even of his soul.

Although they may be beautiful, the words of those who stand apart from Christ are not pure but interspersed with innumerable lies; the words of the Lord alone are pure, in which there is no lie mixed, and they are true as silver purged and proven in the furnace. When anything is declared with them, it is never to be rejected in doubt.

This Judas, then, to whom it was said through the prophet: "But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance," fell, though he had been one of those whom Christ took up for the leadership of the Christian people. And see how that which is written, "But you shall die like men, and you shall fall like one of the princes," is referred now to that prince who fell "like lightning from heaven," now to Judas, who, chosen to the princedom of the apostolate and, as it were, established in heaven, and himself, as it were, set beforehand like lightning, fell, going into the ruin of betrayal (against the one chief of the priests, who had been made "forever" a "priest according to the order of Melchizedek") to many chief priests and adversaries of the one high priest, that he might sell for a price him who willed to redeem the whole world from the curse of the law and of all sin, and…

The Persians therefore may call the "whole circle of heaven" Jupiter; but we maintain that "the heaven" is neither Jupiter nor God, as we indeed know that certain beings of a class inferior to God have ascended above the heavens and all visible nature: and in this sense we understand the words, "Praise God, you heaven of heavens, and you waters that are above the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord."

"Give me remission that I may be refreshed before I depart, and shall be no more, for I am a sojourner": as long as I am with you, so long I am; but if I go forth from you, I have lost even this very thing that I am, and I shall be as one who is not. Thus for this reason he says concerning sinners: "And they shall be as those who are not". And elsewhere: "Who called the things that are not". "Give me remission that I may be refreshed before I depart, and shall be no more". It must be known, nevertheless, that it is within us either to be or not to be. As long as we cleave to God and are joined to him who truly is, we too are. But if we depart from him and do not cleave to our God, we fall by vice into the contrary. Not, therefore, through this is the substantial destruction of the soul designated, but it is said "not to be" when it does not remain in him who truly and always is, from…

When the Lord wipes out those things that are base, he will destroy those very things, so that when those things that have come on a person unexpectedly have been destroyed, the foremost creation of God whom the baser things had overtaken may take up the higher things.

The darts of the evil one are the evil reasonings; and so he will not even be able to cast them into the heart at the outset, whenever someone is sheltered by the shield of faith, since all the fiery darts of the enemy are quenched in it. And the one who is girded about with the shield of faith will say: "In the Lord I have trusted; how will you say to my soul, migrate to the mountains like a sparrow? For behold, the sinners have bent the bow, they have prepared darts for the quiver, to shoot down in the darkness of the moon the upright in heart". For "since I have trusted", he says, "in the Lord, how" do you counsel me not to stand against the "bows" that are "bent" by the sinners against me and the "darts" that are "prepared" by them in their quivers, when they wish to wound "the upright in heart"? For behold, I both stand and do not migrate, and all the fiery darts of the evil one…

"All the day I went about saddened, for my loins are filled with illusions." In the loins or in the reins the receptacle of human seed is said to be; whereby that kind of sin is indicated which is carried out through lust. For its work is that thing which the Apostle designated among the foremost sacrileges, saying: "Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them the members of a harlot? God forbid!" When, therefore, one flows more inclinedly and incontinently into wantonness of this kind, then his loins, or reins, are asserted to be filled with illusions. For it is an illusion of the devil deluding a man and provoking the incontinence of this kind of sin. It is no wonder, then, if the loins of sinful men are filled with illusions, since Job too speaks thus of the dragon, who is understood to be the devil: "All his strength is in the loins, and his power in the navel of his…

"Although man walks about in an image". An image is necessarily the image of something. For Holy Scripture too, when it names an image, sometimes indeed defines it and says whose image it is, but sometimes sets down "image" without any qualification. Thus, concerning the Savior, when it says "who is the image", it did not keep silent whose image he is, but added, saying: "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature". And again, when it teaches us about the diverse images, and that each single person bears some image, it says: "As we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us bear the image of the heavenly". With a qualification—either "of the earthly" or "of the heavenly"—it named the image. But elsewhere it speaks without any qualification, just as in this place it says: "Although man walks about in an image". But in the image of what? Of God, or in the…

But this verse seems to me to contain also another mystery: that the life and manner of living in this world is a kind of imaginary thing and an image, while the future one will not be imaginary but true; and this is what is meant, that each person has an image of virtue, yet does not properly and sincerely live in the virtue itself. Now what we say is of this sort: Wisdom and knowledge are a great part of the virtues; but in the present life, if anyone thinks he has known, he has not yet known as he ought to know, for he who knows, knows in a riddle. Therefore we walk about in an image of knowledge and not in knowledge itself, through which one knows face to face. So likewise we walk about in the image of wisdom, and not yet in wisdom itself, because we do not yet behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. The same things I dare to say concerning the righteousness of God, that we…

There follows: "He treasures up, and knows not for whom he gathers these things". For it was necessary to inquire what those things are that are treasured up while it is unknown for whom they are gathered, and what those things are that are gathered while it is not unknown for whom they remain.

I beseech you to remember in all your present contest the great reward laid up in heaven for those who are persecuted and reviled for righteousness' sake, and to be glad and leap for joy on account of the Son of man, just as the apostles once rejoiced when they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for his name. And if you should ever perceive your soul drawing back, let the mind of Christ, which is in us, say to it, when it wishes to trouble that mind as much as it can, "Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you disquiet me? Hope in God, for I shall yet give him thanks." I pray that our souls may never be disquieted, and even more that in the presence of the tribunals and of the naked swords drawn against our necks they may be guarded by the peace of God, which passes all understanding, and may be quieted when they consider that those who are foreigners from the body are at home…

That also is fulfilled in him which was said: "I will call you back thence at the end." For the end is set down as the perfection of things and the consummation of the virtues. On account of this, in short, another of the saints also said: "do not call me back in the midst of my days." And again Scripture bears witness to the great patriarch Abraham, that "Abraham died full of days." This, then, is "I will call you back thence at the end," as though he said: since "you have fought the good fight, you have kept the faith, you have finished the course," I will now call you back from this world to the future blessedness, to the perfection of eternal life, to "the crown of righteousness, which the Lord will render at the end of the ages to all who love him."

"And the Lord will not forsake His saints, they shall be preserved forever". As he says that he shall dwell forever, so also they shall be preserved forever. Both of which look to the future time, or age, for which the saints shall be preserved, that thereafter they may endure in eternity. "The unjust shall be punished, and the seed of the impious shall perish; but the righteous shall inherit the earth". We have already said above of what sort is the seed of the impious, when we referred it to word and doctrine: and how it shall be exterminated, while every lie is put to flight by the light of truth as darkness. "But the righteous shall inherit the earth". And of this too we have already spoken above, how, whether the righteous or the meek, they attain the inheritance of that good and great land, and how they dwell in it forever and ever — not only forever, but forever and ever. See how…

And if we must make a statement regarding Judas that may overwhelm our opponents with shame, we would say that, in the book of Psalms, the whole of Psalm 108 [LXX] contains a prophecy about Judas, the beginning of which is this: "O God, whom I praise, do not remain silent; for the mouths of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man are opened against me." And it is predicted in this psalm both that Judas separated himself from the number of the apostles on account of his sins and that another was selected in his place; and this is shown by the words "and let another man take his position." But now suppose that he had been betrayed by one of his disciples, who was possessed by a worse spirit than Judas and who had completely poured out, as it were, all the words that he had heard from Jesus, what would this contribute to an accusation against Jesus or the Christian religion? And how…

The expression "you have rebuked" indicates correction: "You have blotted out his name." God blotted out the name Abram, making it Abraham, and Sarai, calling her Sarah, and Simon, naming him Peter. And thus it follows, the name of those are blotted out whom he has rebuked.… Observe, however, that it is not said, You have blotted out their names from the book of the living … but from the pledges that had been signed in the book of debtors or in the book of the dead among the household of the wicked; thus he inscribes the dead, and he registers their names on the earth. The Savior will inscribe the names of his disciples in the heavens.
The outer man has a sense of taste; and the inner man too has a spiritual taste, of which it is said: "Taste and see how good the Lord is."

Seeing them fearful about themselves, He pointed out the betrayer by the evidence of the prophetic voice that says: "he that eateth my bread with me hath magnified his supplanting against me"; for that saying does not differ from this which He says: he that dippeth his hand with me in the dish, the same shall betray me. But I suppose that He said this because He wished to make manifest the greatness of his malice, since the one whom He had received at the common table and who had eaten together with Him (perhaps because in the beginning he was acting well), this very man betrayed Jesus, who was embracing him with such great honors, and became mindful neither of the same salt nor of the table nor of the bread shared in common, but transgressing all those things for the promise of thirty coins he betrayed the bestower of such great goods. And this is truly the peculiar habit of…

Since evil and iniquity may not dwell with you, nor may they remain in your sight, I will enter into your house by your mercy. Then I will be able to say, "Early in the morning I will stand before you, and you will see me." And since I enter into your house by no other way than by your mercy, with great reverence that is called your fear [i.e., the fear of God], I will worship you, having walked in spirit and truth.

"Keep innocence, and behold equity". The word of God commands us to keep innocence. To such a degree has the corruption of morals advanced among men, that among very many innocence is judged as folly: but Scripture judges this to be the work of the highest virtue, because it judges that to be innocence which harms no one, injures no one. When therefore he says: "Keep innocence", this is what he commands us to observe, that we injure no one, harm no one. And this we obtain if always, with an intent and vigilant mind, we behold equity. Equity therefore in this place I take thus, as truth, as righteousness, as life, which is Christ. For by beholding these things, we shall at the same time also behold God. "Keep" therefore "innocence, and behold equity, for there are remnants for the peaceable man". I ask what these remnants are which are reserved for the peaceable man? We are wont to speak…

But from the fig tree learn a parable: for when its branch has now become tender and puts forth leaves, know that summer is near; so also you, when you shall see all these things, know that it is near, at the door. Amen I say to you, that this generation shall not pass away, until all things be done. Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.

How the comparison of the things that have been said can be understood from the fig tree, we shall expound according to our ability: lest perhaps this whole world and its consummation be likened to a fig tree, and each one of those setting out toward the blessed life, so as to see in himself the glorious and perfect coming of Christ's word, be held to be like a fig tree. For just as the fig tree in the time of winter indeed has in itself the life-giving power, but has it hidden and not sufficiently manifest, and afterward,…

No one who stands blasphemes Jesus, nor anyone who walks aright; for it was those passing by who blasphemed him (or, as the Greek has it, those going past), who also, once the fence of the vineyard has been broken down by God, gather as their vintage those who have remained; for it is written: "Why have you cast down its fence, and all who pass by the way gather it as their vintage?" So long, therefore, as anyone has not passed by the way nor turned aside from the way, or, standing, can say to God: you have set "my feet upon a rock", he does not blaspheme Jesus; but if he has fallen or gone past or crossed over or turned aside, then he blasphemes him. As, further, those who have fallen into evil works, and those who have forsaken "the eternal bounds" and the way of the heavenly church, and are tossed and carried about "by every wind of doctrine in the deceit of men, in craftiness for…

I have heard it handed down by the elders that in that parting of the sea individual divisions of the waters were made for each and every tribe of the children of Israel, and that a way was opened in the sea proper to each tribe, and that this is shown from that which is written in the Psalms: "who divided the Red Sea into divisions." By which it is taught that many divisions were made, not one. But also by that which is said: "there is Benjamin the younger in amazement, the princes of Judah their leaders, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali," no less does a proper entrance seem to be enumerated for each tribe. These things, observed by the elders in the divine Scriptures, I have thought it a religious duty not to pass over in silence.

That to lose the hearing is in our power, if we speak of the inner hearing, is asserted also by the prophet, who says: "From their very birth the wicked have gone astray; from the mother's womb they err, speaking lies. Their venom is like the venom of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears and does not hear the voice of the charmer, of the enchantments of the enchanter most skilled in enchantments." You too, when you are aware of your guilt, but having heard the word and the incantation of the enchanter, the one most skilled in enchantments, and having heard the charming words directed to quell your fury and your malice, and even then stop up your ears and do not listen to what is offered you — then it will be said of you: "Their venom is like the venom of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears and does not hear the voice of the charmer."

"But the iniquitous shall be exterminated together", that is, all alike shall be exterminated, because there shall be one end for them, Gehenna. "The remnants of the impious shall perish", then when he who has the power shall give over both body and soul, destroyed, into Gehenna.

One who wishes to know and to act rightly has many adversaries. There are people and demons full of envy whom the good deeds of those acting uprightly torment. The prophet, when he understood this, did not allow himself to fight by his own strength against those who rose up against him, but he called on God to extend his hand by which he could escape unharmed from so many enemies, saying, "You, O Lord, lead me in your righteousness; then it will happen that my path may be directed in your sight."

"And they shall not be confounded in the evil time". But the righteous shall not be confounded in the evil time. And the evil time here he names the time of judgment, because of the multitude of sinners, and of those whom savage torments shall receive. Then therefore, in the time of resurrection, when all have risen, and some shall rise into eternal life, others into eternal confusion, then, he says, the righteous shall not be confounded, because nothing worthy of confusion is found in their acts. But he adds: "And in the days of famine they shall be satisfied". First it must be inquired who are the days of famine. God threatens in a certain place through the prophet, and says: "Behold, the days come, says the Lord, and I will send a famine upon the earth, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst of water, but a famine for hearing the word of God. And they shall go about from the east even…

There is no evening of God possible and, I think, no morning, but the time, if I may put it this way, which is coextensive with his unoriginated and eternal life, is today for him, the day in which the Son has been begotten. Consequently neither the beginning nor the day of his generation is to be found.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 1:204

quotes.quote: After these things there are added certain matters which need no small exposition, for he says: "The sinner shall borrow and shall not repay, but the righteous shows mercy and lends". Even this, if we take it according to the letter, will not seem true. For many sinners indeed receive money on loan and repay it with interest, so that they themselves sometimes have even taken profit from the money which they had received. But here the Prophet defines, saying: "The sinner shall borrow, and shall not pay". But if you understand who it is that lends, and who it is that receives the loan, and inquire who is the sinner that does not repay the money which he received, you will understand that what is written has consistency. For example, when Paul teaches and hearers stand by him, Paul is he who lends the Lord's money, but the hearers are those who receive from his mouth the money of the word…

"The sinners have unsheathed the sword, they have bent their bow, that they may cast down the needy and the poor". Not that in every kind sinners have a bodily sword, but let us see whether perchance, just as there are certain arms of God, among which is said to be the breastplate of righteousness, and the sword of the spirit, and the shield of faith, so also there are arms of the devil, with which the sinful man is clothed. From contraries, therefore, let us understand contraries, and let us set up two armed soldiers, one a soldier of God, the other a soldier of the devil. And if indeed the soldier of God has the breastplate of righteousness, without doubt the soldier of the devil bears the breastplate of unrighteousness contrary to this. And if the soldier of God gleams in the helmet of salvation, on the contrary the sinner who is the soldier of the devil is clothed with the helmet of…

In the preceding treatise we said certain things about the sword and bow of sinners, and about the arms of God, and that all men are armed; and where we said all men, I will now add what was lacking in what preceded, that is, all those who are already able to sin, or to abstain from sins. For infants can handle neither the arms of God nor the arms of the devil. But if any are already able, in word and act and thought, to know what is right and to avoid what is contrary, these are they who are said to have all the arms; and if indeed they sin, they have the arms of the devil and of iniquity; but if they act rightly, they will be said to be clothed with the arms of God. What then he said, "The sinners have drawn the sword, they have bent their bow", we explained, following the Apostle, who spoke from contraries: "And the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God", that the sword of…

"For I proclaim my iniquity". The proclamation of iniquity, that is, the confession of sin, we have spoken of rather often. See, then, what the divine Scripture teaches us: that one ought not to hide sin within. For perhaps, just as those who have shut up within an undigested food, or an abundance of humor or phlegm remaining heavily and troublesomely in the stomach, are relieved if they vomit: so also those who have sinned, if indeed they hide and retain sin within themselves, are pressed within, and are all but suffocated by the phlegm, or humor, of sin. But if one becomes his own accuser, while he accuses and confesses himself, he at once vomits out both the transgression and digests every cause of the disease. Only look around more carefully to whom you ought to confess your sin. First test the physician to whom you ought to lay open the cause of your sickness, who knows how to be…
No one seeking the face of God will see his face and live, … unless he or she has been changed.

If need be, we will not only partake of the blessings of life but bear its appointed sorrows as a trial to our souls. For in this way is divine Scripture accustomed to speak of human afflictions, by which, as gold is tried in the fire, so the human spirit is tried and is found to be worthy either of condemnation or of praise.… We are therefore prepared and are ready to say, "Try me, O Lord, and prove me; purge my reins and my heart."

No one is able to exalt God unless God has lifted him up. For we are lifted up on high through the cross of Christ, who said, "When I will have been lifted up, I will draw all to me." We exalt the Lord who himself exalted the Father, and as much as he has been in him, he shows the Father to the ones who believe. He teaches that there are certain invisible enemies of the human spirit who envy the salvation handed over to them by God. They lie in wait, and they observe whether an error, fall or mishap should happen, which, if it would, straightway they mock that salvation as if joyful with the wrongdoing, against which mockery he bears up with strength if they will see that salvation illuminated by divine steps. He thanks God because God did not allow him to be cast away but corrected him from his fall. One who realizes this clearly exalts God and protects the worthy teaching that comes…

And again that darkness is brought upon men by their evil deeds, we learn from John himself, when he says in his epistle, "If we say that we have fellowship with Him and walk in darkness, we lie and do not the truth," and again, "He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now," and again, "He that hateth his brother is in darkness, and walketh in darkness, and knoweth not whither he goeth, because darkness hath blinded his eyes." Walking in darkness signifies evil conduct, and to hate one's brother, is not that to fall away from that which is properly called knowledge? But he also who is ignorant of divine things walks in darkness, just because of that ignorance; as David says, "They knew not, they understood not, they walk in darkness."
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 2:161

quotes.quote: And note: do you think it was as though inferior to the angels, or needing the help of angels, that the Savior said: or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will furnish me more than twelve legions of angels? — or was it perhaps according to the estimation of Peter, who wished to bring him help and brought forth the sword and cut off the servant's ear, that he spoke such things? For rather do the angels have need of the help of the only-begotten Son of God than he of theirs. For this reason, that which is written, "for he shall give his angels charge concerning you, to keep you in all your ways", is understood to be said not of the only-begotten Son of God, but either in the person of Christ concerning every just man, whom Christ was bearing in his body, or concerning Christ according to his human nature. And finally, that which he says, he will deliver you "from ruin and…

Since the commandment enjoins, saying, "Be subject to the Lord", it seems necessary to examine what it is to be subject to the Lord, and what it is not to be subject. For just as "not everyone who says, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven", so not everyone who says that he is subject to the Lord is subject to him, but he who is in fact subject to him; because that one is truly subject to the Lord whom not the word of profession but the work of subjection shows to be so. And what we say is more fully understood in this way: Our Lord Jesus Christ is righteousness. Therefore no one who acts unrighteously is subject to Christ, who is righteousness. Christ is truth. No liar is subject to Christ, who is truth, whether he speaks falsehood in deeds or in doctrine. The Lord Jesus Christ is sanctification. No one is subject to…

"Do not envy him who prospers in his way, in the man who works iniquity". He describes those things which befall men. For frequently, if we see the unrighteous man in prosperous successes, and placed in that happiness of life which they lead, we are scandalized, and we incur peril of faith, and in our heart we complain against divine Providence, saying: What does it profit to act righteously? Behold, the righteous are afflicted, here the unrighteous man acts prosperously. He is unrighteous, and he arrives at the highest riches, he ascends to the lofty summit of honors and powers; perhaps it is better to be unrighteous than righteous. These things weak and frail souls, even if they do not utter them with the mouth, nevertheless speak in their heart, when they have seen the unrighteous acting in prosperous successes in their way. And therefore the healing of this commandment comes to our…

The expression "we have need" is applied to those things that are necessary for life. Consequently, applied to material things, it means that one does not need most things but only those of which Paul says, "but having food and clothing, we shall be satisfied with these things." Those things, [by contrast], that are accumulated in wealth and luxury are the result of abundance among those who live luxuriously. They are not considered to be necessary and absolutely essential but to be superfluous. So, therefore, there are also things that are necessary for us in the realm of divine matters, which bring us into life and cause us to be in the one who says, "I am the life." But what supersedes these things would be said to supersede need. It is said of such things, "Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart." These include all the things that are considered in…
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 32:106

quotes.quote: "Take delight in the Lord, and he will give you the petitions of your heart". It is the custom of divine Scripture to introduce two men by ὁμωνυμίᾳ, that is, to name the one from the other by likeness of the other — that is, to apply the things which are of the outer man also to the inner. But what I say is this: The outer, corporeal man feeds on corruptible foods, and those suited to him. But there is also a certain food of the inner man, of which it is said that man lives in every word of God. There is a drink of the outer man, there is another of the inner. For we drink from the spiritual rock that follows, and we drink water which, as Jesus says, "whoever drinks, shall not thirst forever". There is also a garment of the outer man, there is also a garment of the inner man. And if indeed he is a sinner, he clothes himself with cursing like a garment. But if he is righteous, he hears:…

And He settled there the hungry, and they established a city for habitation, the church. There He sowed fields according to the fallen seed into good and rich land yielding a hundredfold, and planted vineyards. For the vines are the disciples of the Lord, who also bore fruit of birth. And He blessed them and they multiplied greatly. But the Lord, who saves both humans and animals, did not deem the smallest among them to be insignificant; for it is written: "And He did not diminish their cattle."
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 28:212-15

quotes.quote: I think the daughter of Pharaoh can be seen as the church, which is gathered from the nations, which, although she has an impious and iniquitous father, yet to her it is said through the prophet: "hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and the house of your father, because the king has desired your beauty." This, then, is she who goes out from her father's house and comes to the waters, that she may be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father's house. Finally, straightway she takes up "the bowels of mercy" and has compassion on the infant. This church, therefore, coming from the nations, finds Moses lying in the marsh, cast off by his own and exposed, gives him to be nursed, he is nursed among his own, there he passes his infancy. But when "he has grown stronger," then he is brought to her and adopted as a son.

After these things he admonishes concerning a vice by which almost all of us are troubled, and I know not whether anywhere anyone rare is found so perfect as to be without this disease. "Cease", he says, "from anger, and forsake indignation". There are many vices which are easily avoided by many. For example, the evil of unchastity. If anyone shall have devoted himself more earnestly to the labor of continence, he has cast off unchastity. Some have even subdued avarice, so that, although in other things they are not perfect, they seem nevertheless to avoid this evil, and some others as well. But the vice of wrath, hard and sharp, inflames and agitates even those who seem to be wise. Hence also Solomon says in the Proverbs: "Anger destroys even the prudent". That is, Do not, he says, wonder if wrath inflames the foolish, the evil, the unbelieving man, since frequently wrath agitates good…

They rage, therefore, and dwell on worthless ideas and have gathered themselves and stand united together. Not only by their appearance have they moved the crowds against Christ, but whatever has been done by them is counted as if they had assailed the Father. So, it is said that these had turned against the Lord and his anointed.

But do you wish that I show you from the Scriptures that these several virtues, which we mentioned above, are called trees or shrubs? I bring forward as witness the most wise Solomon, saying concerning wisdom: "it is a tree of life", he says, "to all who embrace it". If therefore "wisdom is a tree of life", without doubt there is also another tree of prudence, and another of knowledge, and another of justice. For it is not consequently said that of all the virtues wisdom alone deserved to be called "a tree of life", but that the other virtues by no means received the appellations of a like lot. "The trees", therefore, "of the field shall give their fruit". This, I believe, blessed David also felt concerning himself, when he said: "but I am like a fruitful olive in the house of God". From which he manifestly shows that a just and holy man is called a tree of olive.

"And you shall sleep and there shall be none to terrify you". Solomon too in the Proverbs said: "for if you sit, you shall be without fear; and if you sleep, you shall gladly take sleep; and you shall not fear the terror coming upon you, nor the assaults of the impious coming upon you". These things he said concerning the just and wise man, and these things are said in the blessing: "you shall sleep, and there shall be none to terrify you". For if I become just, no one can terrify me; I fear nothing else, if I fear God; for "the just man", he says, "is confident as a lion", and therefore he does not fear the lion, the devil, nor "the dragon", Satan, nor "his angels", but says according to David: "I will not fear the nocturnal terror, the arrow flying by day, and the business walking in the darkness, the ruin and the noonday demon". He adds also this: "The Lord is my illumination and my…

Let us see if we cannot conclude in the same way that all the sacred books are one book, but that those outside are the "many books" of the preacher. The proof of this must be drawn from Holy Scripture... Observe, in addition to this, if a proof that the sacred writings are one book, and those of an opposite character many, may not be found in the fact that there is one book of the living from which those who have proved unworthy to be in it are blotted out, as it is written: "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living," while of those who are to undergo the judgment, there are books in the plural, as Daniel says: "The judgment was set, and the books were opened." But Moses also bears witness to the unity of the sacred book, when he says: "If Thou forgive the people their sins, forgive, but if not, then wipe me out of the book which Thou hast written."

quotes.quote: "All the day he has mercy and lends". The righteous man all the day has mercy, and all the day is said to lend: he is free for nothing else than to lend of that money which abounds to him. Shall this too here be thought, that the righteous man sits all the day at his table, and, having money before him, lends it to those suffering need? Perhaps this will be thought to be what was said through Moses: "And thou shalt lend to many nations, but thou thyself shalt not seek a loan". But it is certain that it is spoken of the Lord's money, which is commanded to be paid out to the money-changers, brought forth from the treasuries of the wisdom and knowledge of God, that we may make of five talents ten, of two four. And the more abundant money we have in our soul, so much the more shall we lend all the day. But even now, although I am not righteous, yet this which I speak, I lend you the Lord's…

"I have been young, and now am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread: all the day he has mercy and lends". In the passages above it is said that the sinner borrows and does not repay; here, that the righteous man all the day has mercy and lends. And see how, in contraries, they are matched. The sinner not only borrows, but also, when he has received, does not repay: but the righteous man not only does not borrow, but also lends: and not only once or twice, but all the day he lends — that is, lending through the whole time of his life he has mercy, whence also his seed shall be in blessing.

There were evil thoughts in men, which were for this reason revealed, that, being brought out into the open, they might be destroyed and slain, and cease to be, being dead, and that he who died for us might slay them. For as long as the thoughts were hidden and not brought out into the open, it was impossible for them to be utterly slain. Hence we too, if we have sinned, ought to say: "I have made my sin known to you, and my iniquity I have not hidden. I said: I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord". For if we do this and reveal our sins not only to God but also to those who are able to heal our wounds and sins, our sins will be blotted out by him who says: "behold, I will blot out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist".

quotes.quote: But David too speaks in the same spirit in the Psalms and says: "I made known my iniquity, and I did not cover my sin. I said: I will pronounce against myself my injustice, and you forgave the impiety of my heart". You see, therefore, that "to pronounce the sin" merits the remission of sin. For the devil, forestalled in the accusation, will not be able to accuse us further, and, if we are our own accusers, it profits us unto salvation; but if we wait to be accused by the devil, that accusation turns to our punishment; for he will have companions in gehenna, whom he has convicted as companions of his crimes.

There follows: "But my enemies live, and are strengthened over me". To all which that phrase ought to sound as an undertone: "But I will take thought for my sin". And though I see — for often we sinners, if we see our enemies living more boldly, are saddened, and pour out complaints against the divine providence. But he who wishes to be saved should always answer himself this to all these things: even if "my enemies live, and are strengthened over me", yet I "will take thought for my sin". And though I see that I am a sinner, yet, considering also the sins of others which are perhaps graver, seeing too that they are not anxious for their sins, comparing myself to those who consider nothing at all about their most grievous transgressions, and taking thought for my sin, I have hope in You.

"And they who hate me unjustly are multiplied". It is impossible for one placed in this life not to be held in hatred. Christ Jesus was held in hatred. And why do I say it is impossible for one placed in this life not to be held in hatred? God Himself, who did not come into this life, is held in hatred by some. For if He were not held in hatred, the Prophet would by no means say: "Did I not hate those who hate You, O Lord, and pine away over Your enemies? With perfect hatred I hated them". The Marcionites, and Basilides, and the Valentinians hated God, and hated His words. Since, therefore, God is held in hatred, and Christ is made anathema by the Jews even to this present day, since the Holy Spirit who spoke in the prophets is held in hatred by the heretics, do you wish not to be held in hatred, but to be loved and blessed by all? See lest that sentence find you which says: "Woe when…

But taking such counsel against him, the chief priests of the cult of the letter that kills, and the elders of the ministry of condemnation, bound Jesus, who looses men from their bonds and "says to those who are in bonds: come forth", and who looses those who are fettered and says: "let us break their bonds asunder, and let us cast their yoke from us", and who had loosed from her bonds "the daughter of Abraham" bound by Satan "for eighteen years", so that she who "before could not at all look upward" should now be no longer bent down. And they bound him who willed it, and who, in the very fact that he was bound, was laying an ambush against those very bonds and breaking them, so that now the chief priests and elders of the Jews should have no bonds against men, the Lord evidently breaking them in himself.

"I have been afflicted with miseries and bowed down even to the end." But you may sometimes see the man who has sinned mourning and saddened with the sorrow that is according to the world; for the sorrow that is according to God works repentance unto stable salvation. But this man says that I have been afflicted with miseries and bowed down even to the end. For this reason perhaps the holy Apostle himself, knowing that he had once sinned, says: "Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" For he too sinned when he persecuted the Church of God, on account of which he says: "I am not worthy to be called an apostle." I have been afflicted with miseries, then, he says. He does not say, I am still afflicted. For if my sins have now passed away, I have been afflicted with miseries; but if they remain, and I am conversant in them, I am still afflicted with…

quotes.quote: The timbrel represents the death of fleshly desire because of honesty itself. Dancing is the agreement of reasonable spirits all saying the same thing and in which there are no divisions. The stringed instruments suggest the unison of the voices of moral excellence and the unity of the organ which is the church of God resting on reflective and active minds.

"In rebukes for iniquity you have instructed a man, and you have made his soul waste away like a spider". The soul that sins becomes grosser. For such is the nature of sin, on account of which it is written: "The heart of this people has been made gross". But just as sin makes gross, so on the contrary virtue renders the soul subtle, and—if I may wring out, as it were, a novelty of wording—it wipes away and destroys everything corporeal in it, and renders it more purely incorporeal. But that the soul of the sinner grows gross, and, so to speak, becomes fleshly, is indicated by that which is written: "My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh". Without doubt he names as "flesh" the grosser and sinful souls. If, then, the soul grows gross, so that it becomes flesh, he teaches what remedy God prepares: "In rebukes", he says, "for iniquity you have instructed a man,…

If, then, we turn the discourse back to the nature of that animal, from that aspect by which it unfolds a most subtle work which the eye can scarcely comprehend, the exposition which we explained above will seem apt. But if anyone refers it to that which Isaiah writes in his book, that "they have woven the web of a spider", it is to be taken otherwise: that all the things which the sinner weaves and does, you may know to be as nothing as those things which the spider weaves, though they seem varied and composed, though arranged with a certain exquisite art. How much did those rich men who were before us weave, who gathered riches by various arts and cunning devices, who sought magistracies, honors, consulships with diverse ambition—all these wove the webs of a spider. For as vain, as frivolous as is the weaving of the spider, so were all the things they did, and therefore their souls…

And in this way also the just give up to destruction all their enemies, which are their vices, so that they do not spare even the children, that is, the early beginnings and promptings of evil. In this sense also we understand the language of Psalm 137: "O daughter of Babylon, who is to be destroyed; happy shall he be that rewards you as you have served us; happy shall he be that takes and dashes your little ones against the stones." For "the little ones" of Babylon (which signifies confusion) are those troublesome sinful thoughts that arise in the soul, and one who subdues them by striking, as it were, their heads against the firm and solid strength of reason and truth, is the person who "dashes the little ones against the stones"; and he is therefore truly blessed. God may therefore have commanded people to destroy all their vices utterly, even at their birth, without having enjoined…

And therefore he says: "Wait for the Lord"; that is, if you are afflicted, if you are in straits, if you are in persecutions, "wait for the Lord, and keep his way", and turn aside neither to the right hand nor to the left. For if you wait for the Lord without turning aside, you shall obtain that which follows: "And he will exalt you", he says, "that you may inherit the earth". Frequently have we spoken concerning the holy earth, and concerning the earth which is named as the inheritance of the heavenly promises, whose nature — even its situation — is designated a little more evidently in this verse. For this earth in which we now live is said to be below, according to that which is written: "But God is in heaven above, and you upon the earth below". But that earth which is promised to the righteous as an inheritance is promised to be not below, but above. Therefore to him who waits for…

Now a proof that "grace was poured on his lips" is the fact that although the time he spent in teaching was short, … the world has been filled with this teaching and with the religion that came through him. For there has arisen "in his days" "righteousness and an abundance of peace" lasting until the consummation.

And in another place the prophetic word promises: "If you sleep in the midst of the lots, the wings of a dove covered with silver, and the hinder parts of its back in the greenness of gold". For if we take our rest "in the midst of the lots" of the Old and New Testament, there will be given to us "the wings of a dove covered with silver", that is, the words of God, and "its hinder parts" radiant with the gleam and "greenness" of gold, so that our understanding may be filled with the perceptions of the Holy Spirit—that is, so that our speech and mind may be filled with his coming, and that we may neither say anything nor understand anything except what he has suggested, and that all sanctification, both in heart and in words and in deed, may come from the Holy Spirit in Christ Jesus: to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen.

quotes.quote: The verse clearly teaches that the one who comes to the greatest virtue, to very great security, comes on account of faith in God.… The Savior, recognizing that thousands of the people of the circumcision were going to demand that he be crucified and knowing his own spirit of fearlessness (I say these things speaking in terms of the flesh), is able to say even these words.

Christians have nothing to fear, even if demons should not be well-disposed to them; for they are protected by the supreme God, who is well pleased with their piety and who sets his divine angels to watch over those who are worthy of such guardianship, so that they can suffer nothing from demons. He who by his piety possesses the favor of the Most High, who has accepted the guidance of Jesus, the "angel of the great counsel," being well contented with the favor of God through Christ Jesus, may say with confidence that he has nothing to suffer from the whole host of demons.

He who confesses to God for his sins, and grieves in spirit while he repents, knowing what punishment threatens the sinner after the departure from this life, speaks these words, setting forth how much he who turns himself to repentance and amendment must suffer, how his friends and neighbors abandon him and are made distant, because he himself has turned to the confession (exomologesis) of his sin and to mourning. He says, then: "My friends and my neighbors drew near against me and stood". Understand for me a man who is faithful, indeed, but nevertheless weak, who could even be overcome by some sin, and who on this account groans over his transgressions, and in every way seeks the care and healing of his wound; even though he has been caught off guard and has fallen, he still wills to recover his healing and salvation. If, then, a man of this kind, mindful of his transgression,…

Generally there are three types: the first type is the one who does not acknowledge the truth at all, but, as chance has it, when he hands himself over to the vain and unsubstantiated musings of his own heart, he becomes like a wild beast, neither standing nor supported by anything, and accordingly, not sitting. This one, indeed, is said to walk in the counsel of the wicked.

Here is the great cry that reaches up to God. It is not that cry people make resulting from some intense release of air, but it is the pure and untouched outpouring of the words of the inner mind, which extend even to God. It must be realized there is a certain voice in the innermost heart which is not used as an organ of the body, but which a person, after he has entered his bedchamber and settled himself, cries out beyond his own body from the hidden gate of his feelings to him who alone is able to hear a voice of this type. Even if we do not read that Moses cried out with an audible voice, nevertheless it is said by God in Exodus: "Why do you cry to me?" It is the voice of every exile who cries to God about having earthly and ever-changing affairs. The Savior excludes this cry for approaching the Father when he says: "Seek great things, and the small things will be added to you. Seek…

"But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord". But better does it say in the Greek: "But the salvation of the righteous is with the Lord". He did not say, in heaven is the salvation of the righteous, for this too passes away; not with any creature, because nothing is immovable or unchangeable: but with the Lord is the salvation of the righteous, who always remains, is always the same, is always immovable, nor anywhere can the salvation of man be more securely than with the Lord. Let that be for me the place, that for me the house, that for me the dwelling, that the rest, that the habitation. In fine, there is announced to us by holy Scripture not only the kingdom of heaven, but the kingdom of God. As I remember myself to have often said already, the kingdom of heaven is of those who are still in their advances; but the kingdom of God, of those who have already come to the…

There is no other reason for Christ's death (nor was there) than that he was king of the Jews, concerning which he also spoke, saying: "but I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain". The chief of the priests indeed, according to the letter of the law, bore upon his head the shape of a sign, "the sanctification of the Lord" written on the plate, but the true chief of the priests and king, Jesus, on the cross indeed has written: this is the king of the Jews, yet ascending to the Father and receiving the Father into himself, in place of letters and in place of a name he has him who is named, and he has him as a crown.

"The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes." By keeping the commandments of the Lord we do not become more sighted bodily, but by keeping the divine commandments we become more keen-sighted spiritually.

Where should you stand, you who seek sanctification from God? The writer says, "You have established my feet on the rock." "Christ was the rock." Let us learn about the one who follows these promises.

What other light of God can we speak of, in which a person sees light, except God's spiritual power, which when it lightens a person causes him either to see clearly the truth of all things or to know God, who is called the truth? Such then is the meaning of the saying, "In your light shall we see light"; that is, in your word and your wisdom, which is your Son, in him shall we see you, the Father.

"I have spoken", he says, "with my tongue". Let us consider what he has spoken with his tongue: for it seems to me that through these things he indicates something mystical. He says therefore: "Make known to me, O Lord, my end, and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what is lacking to me". If, he says, thou hast made known my end to me, and hast made known to me how great is the number of my days, I shall be able through these things to know also that other thing, what is lacking to me. Or perhaps through these things this too will seem to be indicated, that just as there is some end of every art — for example, the end of building is to make a house; of ship-building, to construct a ship which can overcome the waves of the sea and bear the assaults of the winds; and of each art there is some such end, on account of which the art itself seems to have been devised: so…

Often, we communicate by the lifting of hands, as when Moses' arms were lifted up and Israel was victorious. When his hands were down, the Amalekites won.… Our hands are our deeds of piety. If we store treasures in heaven, we have hands lifted to God and overcome the enemy. When, therefore, I raise my hands to God, I lift my spirit to him through my uplifted hands. Amalek is conquered by me. So, it is needful to lift your hands to God. The temple of God is his glory.

"Because the Lord loves judgment, and will not forsake His saints". How does the Lord love judgment? In that nothing is done with Him without judgment, nothing without reason. So therefore do thou also, knowing that the Lord loves judgment, do all things with just and true judgment, hearing Him who admonishes thee, saying: "Do all things with counsel, drink wine with counsel".

Just as certain rewards are given to the contender in mighty contests, so also in any trial, when that which afflicts is nearby and the powers of the adversaries bring tribulation, know that a spiritual and intellectual table is prepared on account of this trial. Therefore, however many times you will be afflicted, equally many times a spiritual table is placed before you. Fix firm your eyes attentive only to my tables, and, giving thanks, you may say with the apostle, "Not I alone, but we are made glorious in tribulation."

This bread that God the Word declares is his body is the word that feeds souls, word proceeding from God the Word and bread from heavenly Bread. It has been placed on the table about which was written, "You have prepared a table in my sight against those who afflict me." And this drink that God the Word declares is his blood is the word that gives drink and wonderfully intoxicates the hearts of those who drink. This is the cup concerning which was written, "and your intoxicating cup, how glorious it is!" Also, this drink is the fruit of the true Vine, who said, "I am the true vine," and it is the blood of that Grape that produced this drink when it was cast into the winepress of the passion, just as the bread too is the word of Christ, made from that Wheat that "falling into the earth … produces much fruit." For God the Word was not saying that the visible bread that he was holding in…

quotes.quote: And he adds: "Behold, thou hast set my days as old ones". In the Greek it is written, παλαιστάς, which signifies a measure of four fingers. Wishing therefore to teach us who now in this life lead brief and very few days, he spoke this verse of which we spoke above. From which it is understood that another too could say, that Thou hast set my days one finger, as following upon the brevity of time, and another two fingers or three. But I ask whether any of men can say, that My days are ten fingers, or twenty, or even more. And because we come upon difficult passages, I would wish to inquire whether somewhere in the Scriptures we find any such thing, from which that which seems obscure could be opened up more plainly. In Isaiah I remember it is written: "Who has measured", he says, "the water with his hand, and the heaven with a span, and all the earth with his fist"? From which let…

He also adds in what follows and says: "My substance is as nothing before thee". Unless he had added before thee, I should be greatly grieved, for the reason that he had said the human substance to be nothing. But now, because he said before thee, it is as if he said that in comparison indeed either with the angels or with the rest of the creatures, my substance is not abject, nor least. In short, even if we act well, and keep the commandments of the Lord, we are invited to the fellowship of the angels: "They shall be", he says, "as the angels of God in heaven". But in comparison with God, even if I be Peter, against whom the gates of hell shall not prevail, my substance before him is nothing. And he used sufficiently the proper term of nature. For all is nothing, however great it be, whatever is out of nothing, for he alone is the one who is, and who always is. But our substance is as…

But in what follows, as if explaining this very thing which he said, that "my substance is as nothing before thee", he added and says: "Nevertheless the whole is vanity, every living man". How do you take "living"? If indeed we think true life to be vanity, why do we labor? But see whether perhaps this which he says, every living man, is to be taken of this present life, as it is written, and we shall prove it by testimonies. For all things that are in this life among men are vain, even if Moses be in this life, for he too knows in part, and prophesies in part, and sees through a mirror and in an enigma, and knows a shadow, and is taught figures, and does not yet see the truth, and therefore he is indeed living, but his life is vanity. And do you wish to see that it is vanity? "When that which is perfect shall have come, those things which are in part shall be destroyed". But all that…

Let us therefore see whether some also of the ancient saints did not hold an opinion of the tabernacle far other than these men now reckon. For hear how magnificently David, that surpassing one among the prophets, thinks concerning the tabernacle: "While it is said" he says "to me every day: Where is thy God? these things have I remembered, and I have poured out my soul within me, for I shall enter into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God". But now, Jesus no longer walks openly among the Jews, and He has departed from them, and there is no word of God among the Jews. quotes.quote: Now "the Holy Spirit descended upon" the Savior "in the form of a dove", a bird that is gentle, innocent, and simple. Whence it is also commanded to us that we should imitate the innocence of doves. Such is the Holy Spirit—clean and winged and rising to the heights. Wherefore in prayer we say: "Who will give me wings like a dove's, and I shall fly and be at rest?"—that is: who will give me the wings of the Holy Spirit?

quotes.quote: "When he shall have fallen", he says, "he shall not be troubled". Having above said that his steps are directed by the Lord, here he speaks of his fall. See, then, that even to those who travel this journey it sometimes happens to fall, even to those who are directed by the Lord; but there is a great difference between the fall of the righteous and the fall of the unrighteous. The righteous man, he says, when he shall have fallen, is not laid prostrate; the unrighteous man, and he who has no hope placed in God, if he shall have fallen, is laid prostrate and does not rise — that is, if he has sinned, he does not repent and knows not how to amend his sin. But the righteous man, if he has offended in anything, if in a word — for it is the Apostle who says: "For in many things we all offend, and if any man offend not in word, this is a perfect man" — the righteous man therefore offends in…

Is God a light to enlighten the eyes of the body or the eyes of the intellect? The prophet says of the latter, "Enlighten my eyes lest I sleep in death." I think it is clear to everyone that we would not say that God performs the work of the sun and assigns to another the task of enlightening the eyes of those who will not sleep in death. God, therefore, enlightens the mind of those whom he judges to be worthy of personal enlightenment. But if God illuminates the mind according to the statement "The Lord is my light," then we must assume that he is apprehended by the intellect and is invisible and incorporeal, because he is the light of the mind.

"In many portions and in many ways God spoke to the fathers in the prophets". Sometimes indeed he teaches us ineffable mysteries in the things he speaks; but sometimes he instructs us concerning the Savior and his coming; and at other times he corrects and amends our conduct. On this account we shall attempt to assign, throughout the several passages of divine Scripture, distinctions of this kind, and to discern where there are prophecies and something is said about things to come, where certain mystical things are indicated, and where the passage is moral. Beginning therefore the exposition of the thirty-sixth psalm, we find that this whole psalm is moral, and given as it were as a certain care and medicine for the human soul, since it reproves our sins and teaches us to live according to the law. But let us now see what sort of beginning the first verse gives us. "Be not", he says,…
At first this one makes many plans in his soul, but in the end [see v. 5], he rests in the great plan of God for everyone, whose spirit is in the root of Jesse.

Hear also elsewhere how God plants. The prophet says: "You transferred a vine out of Egypt, you cast out the nations and planted it. You made a way passable before it, you planted its roots, and it filled the earth. Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God." He is raised up above himself who departs from the traces of his elders and tries to have vision in things that are beyond his powers. Hence, it follows, "If I was not humbly minded, but exalted my soul: as a child that is weaned is towards his mother, so will you reward my soul." And so it is useful for us to think humble thoughts, in the words of the apostle: "Not setting your mind on high things but condescending to the lowly"; and to receive weaning with Isaac, that we may share stronger food rather than with Ishmael, son of the slave girl, to carry a bottle with water instead of wine and to be driven from the eternal…

Solomon was not the Lord of hosts. But, when our Christ arose from the dead and ascended into heaven, the heavenly princes chosen by God were ordered to open the gates of heaven that the King of glory might enter and sit at the right hand of the Father until he makes his enemies his footstool. Now, when these heavenly princes saw that he was in appearance without beauty, honor or glory, and not recognizing him, they asked, "Who is this King of glory?" And the Holy Spirit, either in his own name or in the Father's, answered, "The Lord of hosts. He is the King of glory." But I am sure that everyone will admit that none of the gatekeepers of the temple at Jerusalem ever said of Solomon (though he was ever so glorious a king) or of the ark of testimony, "Who is this King of glory?"

And as they kept silence, I went on: "[The Scripture], speaking by David about this Christ, my friends, said no longer that `in His seed' the nations should be blessed, but `in Him.' So it is here: `His name shall rise up for ever above the sun; and in Him shall all nations be blessed.' But if all nations are blessed in Christ, and we of all nations believe in Him, then He is indeed the Christ, and we are those blessed by Him. God formerly gave the sun as an object of worship, as it is written, but no one ever was seen to endure death on account of his faith in the sun; but for the name of Jesus you may see men of every nation who have endured and do endure all sufferings, rather than deny Him. For the word of His truth and wisdom is more ardent and more light-giving than the rays of the sun, and sinks down into the depths of heart and mind. Hence also the Scripture said, `His name…

Further, to persuade you that you have not understood anything of the Scriptures, I will remind you of another psalm, dictated to David by the Holy Spirit, which you say refers to Solomon, who was also your king. But it refers also to our Christ. But you deceive yourselves by the ambiguous forms of speech. For where it is said, 'The law of the Lord is perfect,' you do not understand it of the law which was to be after Moses, but of the law which was given by Moses, although God declared that He would establish a new law and a new covenant. And where it has been said, 'O God, give Thy judgment to the king,' since Solomon was king, you say that the Psalm refers to him, although the words of the Psalm expressly proclaim that reference is made to the everlasting King, i.e., to Christ. For Christ is King, and Priest, and God, and Lord, and angel, and man, and captain, and stone, and a Son…

Then Trypho said, "We know that you quoted these because we asked you. But it does not appear to me that this Psalm which you quoted last from the words of David refers to any other than the Father and Maker of the heavens and earth. You, however, asserted that it referred to Him who suffered, whom you also are eagerly endeavouring to prove to be Christ."

And I answered, "Attend to me, I beseech you, while I speak of the statement which the Holy Spirit gave utterance to in this Psalm; and you shall know that I speak not sinfully, and that we are not really bewitched; for so you shall be enabled of yourselves to understand many other statements made by the Holy Spirit. 'Sing unto the Lord a new song; sing unto the Lord, all the earth: sing unto the Lord, and bless His name; show forth His salvation from day to day, His wonderful works among all people.' He bids the inhabitants of all…

And that God the Father of all would bring Christ to heaven after He had raised Him from the dead, and would keep Him there until He has subdued His enemies the devils, and until the number of those who are foreknown by Him as good and virtuous is complete, on whose account He has still delayed the consummation-hear what was said by the prophet David. These are his words: "The Lord said unto My Lord, Sit Thou at My right hand, until I make Thine enemies Thy footstool. The Lord shall send to Thee the rod of power out of Jerusalem; and rule Thou in the midst of Thine enemies. With Thee is the government in the day of Thy power, in the beauties of Thy saints: from the womb of morning have I begotten Thee." That which he says, "He shall send to Thee the rod of power out of Jerusalem," is predictive of the mighty word, which His apostles, going forth from Jerusalem, preached everywhere; and…
These words also show clearly that he who did all things [God the Father] testified that he [Jesus] is to be worshiped both as God and Christ.

And from the ninety-fifth (ninety-sixth) Psalm they have taken away this short saying of the words of David: "From the wood." For when the passage said, "Tell ye among the nations, the Lord hath reigned from the wood," they have left, "Tell ye among the nations, the Lord hath reigned." Now no one of your people has ever been said to have reigned as God and Lord among the nations, with the exception of Him only who was crucified, of whom also the Holy Spirit affirms in the same Psalm that He was raised again, and freed from [the grave], declaring that there is none like Him among the gods of the nations: for they are idols of demons.

If, sirs, it were not said by the Scriptures which I have already quoted, that His form was inglorious, and His generation not declared, and that for His death the rich would suffer death, and with His stripes we should be healed, and that He would be led away like a sheep; and if I had not explained that there would be two advents of His,-one in which He was pierced by you; a second, when you shall know Him whom you have pierced, and your tribes shall mourn, each tribe by itself, the women apart, and the men apart,-then I must have been speaking dubious and obscure things. But now, by means of the contents of those Scriptures esteemed holy and prophetic amongst you, I attempt to prove all [that I have adduced], in the hope that some one of you may be found to be of that remnant which has been left by the grace of the Lord of Sabaoth for the eternal salvation. In order, therefore, that…

And that God the Father of all would bring Christ to heaven after He had raised Him from the dead, and would keep Him there until He has subdued His enemies the devils, and until the number of those who are foreknown by Him as good and virtuous is complete, on whose account He has still delayed the consummation-hear what was said by the prophet David. These are his words: "The Lord said unto My Lord, Sit Thou at My right hand, until I make Thine enemies Thy footstool. The Lord shall send to Thee the rod of power out of Jerusalem; and rule Thou in the midst of Thine enemies. With Thee is the government in the day of Thy power, in the beauties of Thy saints: from the womb of morning have I begotten Thee." That which he says, "He shall send to Thee the rod of power out of Jerusalem," is predictive of the mighty, word, which His apostles, going forth from Jerusalem, preached everywhere; and…

For your teachers have ventured to refer the passage, "The Lord says to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, till I make Thine enemies Thy footstool," to Hezekiah; as if he were requested to sit on the right side of the temple, when the king of Assyria sent to him and threatened him; and he was told by Isaiah not to be afraid. Now we know and admit that what Isaiah said took place; that the king of Assyria desisted from waging war against Jerusalem in Hezekiah's days, and the angel of the Lord slew about 185,000 of the host of the Assyrians. But it is manifest that the Psalm does not refer to him. For thus it is written, "The Lord says to my Lord, Sit at My right hand, till I make Thine enemies Thy footstool. He shall send forth a rod of power over Jerusalem, and it shall rule in the midst of Thine enemies. In the splendour of the saints before the morning star have I begotten Thee. The Lord…

I, on my part, now wish to engage with you in a discussion on the allegorical expressions of the apostle. What figures of speech could the novel god have found in the prophets (fit for himself)? "He led captivity captive," says the apostle. With what arms? In what conflicts? From the devastation of what country? From the overthrow of what city? What women, what children, what princes did the Conqueror throw into chains? For when by David Christ is sung as "girded with His sword upon His thigh," or by Isaiah as "taking away the spoils of Samaria and the power of Damascus," you make Him out to be really and truly a warrior confest to the eye. Learn then now, that His is a spiritual armour and warfare, since you have already discovered that the captivity is spiritual, in order that you may further learn that this also belongs to Him.
quotes.source_title: The Five Books Against Marcion, Book V, Chapter XVIII

quotes.quote: God spared not his own Son for you, letting him become a curse for us; for "cursed is he who hangs on a tree"; … that he might redeem us from our sins. The sun was darkened on the day of our redemption; hell lost its right to us, and we were enrolled for heaven. The eternal gates were lifted up that the King of glory, the Lord of might, might enter in, and humankind, born of the earth, destined for hell, was purchased for heaven.
quotes.source_title: ON FLIGHT IN TIME OF PERSECUTION 12:2

quotes.quote: True, Scripture says, "Make no mention of the name other gods, neither let it be heard out of your mouth." What it stipulates is that we should not call them gods. For in the first part of the law it says, "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain," that is, apply it to an idol. So anyone who honors an idol with the name of God falls into idolatry. If I am compelled to mention gods, I must add something to show that I do not call them gods. Scripture uses the name "gods" but adds "their" or "of the pagans," as when David, having used the name "gods," says "but the gods of the pagans are demons."

For if the earth has to suffer either joy or injury, it is simply on people's account, that they may suffer the joy or the sorrow through the events that happen to their dwelling place, whereby they will rather have to pay the penalty that, simply on their account, even the earth must suffer. When, therefore, God even threatens the earth, I would prefer saying that he threatens the flesh. So likewise, when he makes a promise to the earth, I would rather understand him as promising the flesh; as in that passage of David: "The Lord is King, let the earth be glad," meaning the flesh of the saints, to which appertains the enjoyment of the kingdom of God.
quotes.source_title: ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 26

quotes.quote: "For the eyes of the Lord are on those who fear him, on those who hope in his mercy, to deliver their souls from death," even eternal death, "and to nourish them in their hunger," that is, after eternal life. "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the Lord delivers them out of them all." "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." "The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them shall be broken." The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants. We have adduced these few quotations from a mass of the Creator's Scriptures; and no more, I suppose, are needed to prove him to be a most good God, for they sufficiently indicate both the precepts of his goodness and the firstfruits of it.

Besides the generally known fact that the riches of the East, that is to say, its strength and resources, usually consist of gold and spices, it is certainly true of the Creator that he makes gold the riches of the other nations also. Thus he says by Zechariah, "And Judah shall also fight at Jerusalem and shall gather together all the wealth of the nations round about, gold and silver." Moreover, respecting that gift of gold, David also says, "And there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia"; and again, "The kings of Arabia and Saba shall offer to him gifts." For the East generally regarded the magi as kings; and Damascus was anciently deemed to belong to Arabia, before it was transferred to Syrophoenicia on the division of the Syrias [by Rome]. Its riches Christ then received, when he received the tokens thereof in the gold and spices; while the spoils of Samaria were the magi…

In various ways has the devil rivalled and resisted the truth. Sometimes his aim has been to destroy the truth by defending it. He maintains that there is one only Lord, the Almighty Creator of the world, in order that out of this doctrine of the unity he may fabricate a heresy. He says that the Father Himself came down into the Virgin, was Himself born of her, Himself suffered, indeed was Himself Jesus Christ. Here the old serpent has fallen out with himself, since, when he tempted Christ after John's baptism, he approached Him as "the Son of God;" surely intimating that God had a Son, even on the testimony of the very Scriptures, out of which he was at the moment forging his temptation: "If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread." Again: "If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down from hence; for it is written, He shall give His angels charge concerning…
